mcqs.question: Why does the 12-factor app methodology insist on reading configuration from the environment rather than hardcoding it in the build?
options: It lets the exact same build artifact run unchanged across dev, staging, and prod
It makes the code shorter to write
Environment variables are faster to read than config files
It's required for the app to be stateless
mcqs.explanation: The point of externalizing config is that one build can be promoted across environments without rebuilding — only the environment differs. It's unrelated to statelessness or read speed; those are separate concerns.

mcqs.question: An app stores user session data in each instance's local memory. What breaks if you try to scale it horizontally behind a load balancer?
options: Nothing — load balancers automatically replicate session data
A user's next request may hit a different instance that has no record of their session, breaking their session
Horizontal scaling always requires rewriting the entire app in a new language
This only becomes a problem if you scale vertically instead
mcqs.explanation: Local in-memory session state ties a user to whichever instance they first hit — the load balancer has no way to guarantee that. Statelessness (session data in a shared store) is what makes any instance able to serve any request.

mcqs.question: A legacy app writes uploaded files to local disk and holds sessions in memory. What are the two changes that make it cloud-native without a full rewrite?
options: Rewrite the whole app in a different programming language
Just add more local disk space to each instance
Move sessions to a shared cache and uploads to object storage, so no instance holds irreplaceable state
Switch to vertical scaling to avoid the session problem entirely
mcqs.explanation: Relocating state (sessions, uploads) out of the instance and into shared backing services is usually enough to make an existing app cloud-native — the app logic itself often doesn't need to change. More local disk or vertical scaling don't solve the underlying single-instance dependency.
